Https defines that using which rules any of the browsers like chrome or Firefox will communicate with any of the websites of webserver like AWS 

Similarly MCP defines that  how our AI application like AI chatbot will communicate with different tools, databases or applications.


Option 1: Clear and Professional (Recommended)

HTTPS defines the rules that web browsers—like Chrome or Firefox—use to communicate with websites and web servers, such as those on AWS.

Similarly, MCP (Model Context Protocol) defines how AI applications, like chatbots, communicate with different tools, databases, and external applications.

Option 2: Concise and Punchy

Just as HTTPS standardizes how web browsers (like Chrome) talk to web servers (like AWS), MCP standardizes how AI chatbots connect to tools, databases, and apps.

MCP(Model Context Protocol) lets our AI models connect to external tools, to databases, to different applications through a single protocol rather than multiple custom integrations and due to this the only reason it makes it simpler for AI applications to switch to tools or to switch the LLM.
Means now if we want to use a different LLM from an existing one in our AI application, than we just need to change a single line of code rather than doing all different custom integrations with APIs again and again on every switch.

Option 1: Clear and Professional (Recommended)

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) allows AI models to connect to external tools, databases, and applications through a single protocol, eliminating the need for multiple custom integrations. Because of this, it is much simpler to switch between different tools or LLMs. For instance, if you want to swap out the existing LLM in your application, you only need to change a single line of code instead of rewriting custom API integrations every time.

Option 2: Concise and Punchy (Great for Presentations or Pitches)

MCP provides a unified protocol for connecting AI models to tools, databases, and apps, replacing fragmented custom integrations. This makes switching tools or LLMs incredibly simple. Instead of rebuilding API integrations from scratch whenever you change an LLM, you can now swap models with just a single line of code.

So, to develop a much cleaner brute force than the initial proposed, we change the search. Instead of looping through numbers until one of them multiplies by x to give some 1, 11, 111, 1111 (in general (10^n-1)/9), we instead loop through such n until we find a (10^n-1)/9 divisible by x, then divide by x.

Already, we've reduced this problem by an exponential amount. But let's reduce it further. We want to find an n such that (10^n-1)/9 is divisible by x. We don't need to find the smallest such n, just any such n.

x | (10^n-1)/9
9x | 10^n-1
10^n-1 % 9x = 0
10^n % 9x = 1

Since x ends in 1, 3, 5, or 7, it shares no factors with 10. Thus, there exists such an n. We can use the Euler's totient function φ(9x). So, (10^φ(9x)-1)/9 should be a multiple of x. Therefore, an integer we can multiply x by to get all 1s is

(10^φ(9x)-1)/(9x).

And we're done.



Note: The number you'll get will probably be quite large. If you wanted to try making the number smaller, you could try using the Carmichael totient γ(9x) instead. It's defined as γ(n) = the smallest positive integer such that, for all m coprime to n, m^γ(n)=1. On top of that, if 10 is what's called a "quadratic residue" of 9x, that means it's the square of something mod 9x, meaning you'd only have to raise it to γ(9x)/2, since that's (something^2)^(γ(9x)/2) = (something)^γ(9x) = 1. Following this logic, if it's a cubic residue, you'd only need γ(9x)/3, and in general, the smallest power you'd have to raise 10 to (other than 0) would definitely be a factor of γ(9x). The smallest such answer is (10^(that factor)-1)/(9x).

We claim any number A that ends in 1, 3, 7, or 9 can be multiplied by some B such that AB has only 1s and 0s.
